paragraphs: The minimum enclosing ball problem asks for a small ball covering a collection of points. This paper studies a differentially private approximation, where protecting information about individual points changes the achievable balance between ball size and coverage. The authors introduce an iterative algorithm that improves both runtime and the utility bound over the previously best known private approximation scheme.

For n points in d dimensions, the returned radius is at most 1 + gamma times the optimal radius. The algorithm may leave some points uncovered: its bound scales as sqrt(d)/(gamma epsilon), apart from hidden logarithmic factors. Its runtime scales as n/gamma², also up to logarithmic factors. Thus, the result combines near-optimal radius with an explicit allowance for uncovered points.

A local-privacy version has an uncovered-point bound scaling as sqrt(nd)/(gamma epsilon). This improves the earlier dependence on n, at the expense of other parameters. The paper also reports empirical testing. Its central contribution is a more efficient private approximation with quantified radius and coverage guarantees.
neurips-2022-a-differentially-private-li.tldr: An iterative private algorithm approximates the minimum enclosing ball with improved runtime and explicit bounds on how many points it may exclude.

paragraphs: This paper compares classification losses through the geometry of the features they produce in a network's final layer. Its focus is neural collapse: examples from the same class share a class mean, while different class means become equally separated. Earlier results connected this geometry to cross entropy and mean squared error; the authors extend the analysis to a broader family, including label smoothing and focal loss.

Under the unconstrained feature model assumption, the paper analyzes optimal solutions and the surrounding optimization landscape. Neural collapse solutions are the only global minimizers in the stated analyses. Other critical points have directions of negative curvature, with a global landscape result for label smoothing and a local result for focal loss near an optimum.

Experiments find largely identical test performance from neural collapse features across the four losses when networks are sufficiently large and trained to convergence. The conclusion is conditional: these losses can produce equivalent training features and similar test behavior in that regime, rather than establishing a universally best loss.
neurips-2022-are-all-losses-created-equa.tldr: Several common classification losses yield equivalent neural collapse features under the analyzed conditions and similar test performance in sufficiently large, converged networks.

paragraphs: Knowledge-intensive language systems need to retrieve evidence as well as generate answers. This paper applies autoregressive language models directly to retrieval by letting them generate text that identifies relevant passages. The goal is to make advances in language generation useful for search with only small changes to model architecture.

Instead of assigning each passage a unique identifier within a hierarchy, the method treats all of its ngrams, or contiguous text sequences, as possible identifiers. The model generates and scores distinctive sequences, and an efficient data structure maps those sequences back to complete passages. A passage can therefore be reached through multiple pieces of its own text, without imposing a hierarchical organization on the search space.

On KILT passage retrieval, the method outperforms earlier autoregressive approaches and reports an average improvement of at least ten points over established retrieval solutions. It also reaches new best downstream results on some datasets while using substantially less memory than competing systems. These findings support passage text itself as a useful retrieval identifier.
neurips-2022-autoregressive-search-engin.tldr: Generating distinctive passage substrings gives autoregressive models an effective, memory-efficient way to retrieve supporting documents.

paragraphs: In decentralized learning, clients communicate with neighboring clients over a fixed network. Sending fewer bits can reduce communication demands, but compression can also slow optimization. This paper addresses that tension for nonconvex problems, particularly when different clients hold substantially different data. Such heterogeneity appears explicitly in the earlier convergence rate discussed by the authors.

BEER combines compressed communication with gradient tracking. The tracking component accompanies the compressed exchanges so that the method can retain a faster convergence rate. The paper proves a rate of O(1/T), where T counts communication rounds, improving on the previously stated O((G/T)^(2/3)) rate, where G measures differences between clients' data.

The new rate matches the uncompressed counterpart even under arbitrary data heterogeneity. This means compression need not worsen the convergence-rate order in the analyzed setting. Numerical experiments support the theoretical result and report practical advantages when client data differ. The contribution links reduced communication to stronger optimization guarantees rather than treating those goals separately.
neurips-2022-beer-fast-o-1-t-rate-for-de.tldr: BEER combines communication compression and gradient tracking to match an uncompressed O(1/T) convergence rate despite heterogeneous client data.

paragraphs: Black-box learning must improve a model using loss evaluations without access to derivatives. This paper analyzes how well such learning generalizes beyond its training data. It studies Zeroth-order Stochastic Search, which substitutes differences between perturbed loss evaluations for stochastic gradient directions. Each example query uses K + 1 evaluations of a model with d parameters.

Assuming the unknown loss is Lipschitz and smooth, the authors derive generalization bounds for bounded and unbounded losses that may be nonconvex. With appropriately chosen, slightly reduced learning rates, these bounds match those for stochastic gradient descent. The bounds themselves do not depend on model dimension, the number of perturbations, or batch size.

A stronger special case applies to bounded nonconvex losses with one example per batch: both the learning rate and generalization error are independent of d and K, remaining essentially comparable to stochastic gradient descent even with two evaluations. Full-dataset batches also recover gradient-descent generalization guarantees. The results clarify when derivative-free updates can retain familiar generalization bounds.
neurips-2022-black-box-generalization-st.tldr: Under smoothness and Lipschitz assumptions, derivative-free stochastic search can match stochastic gradient descent's generalization bounds with suitable learning rates.

paragraphs: BYOL-Explore addresses exploration in environments where visual observations are complex and useful progress can be difficult to discover. It uses curiosity-driven learning to help an agent seek experience, rather than depending only on rewards supplied by the task. The paper's central design choice is to connect representation learning, prediction of world dynamics, and exploration through one prediction loss.

That loss operates in a latent space, meaning the model predicts within a learned representation of its observations. The world representation, dynamics model, and exploration policy are learned together without an additional auxiliary objective. The resulting intrinsic reward is combined with the environment's extrinsic reward to guide behavior.

On DM-HARD-8, a visually rich benchmark with partial observability and continuous actions, this combination solves most tasks; the prior work described required human demonstrations to make progress. The method also achieves superhuman performance on the ten hardest Atari exploration games. These results provide evidence for the approach across two different settings while retaining a comparatively simple design.
neurips-2022-byol-explore-exploration-by.tldr: BYOL-Explore uses a single latent prediction loss to learn representations, dynamics, and curiosity-driven exploration with strong results on difficult exploration benchmarks.

paragraphs: Evaluating a new decision policy from data collected by another policy often centers on its expected outcome. An average, however, does not describe how widely individual outcomes can vary. This paper addresses that gap in contextual bandits, where decisions depend on the available context, by predicting intervals for outcomes under a new target policy.

The proposed method, conformal off-policy prediction, applies conformal prediction to data gathered by a behavioral policy. Its output is a predictive interval rather than only an estimate of average performance. This changes the evaluation question from how well a policy performs on average to what range of outcomes its use may produce.

The authors establish finite-sample guarantees without adding assumptions beyond the standard contextual bandit setup. These guarantees apply at finite data sizes rather than only asymptotically, which motivates their relevance to safety-critical decisions. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the method's utility against existing approaches. The contribution joins outcome variability and finite-sample reliability in off-policy assessment.
neurips-2022-conformal-off-policy-predic.tldr: COPP predicts outcome intervals for a new contextual-bandit policy from another policy's data, with finite-sample guarantees.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial networks can struggle when the available training data are limited relative to their dimensionality. Existing remedies include augmentation, regularization, pretrained models, and pruning, but some depend on particular resources or increase training time. DigGAN introduces a regularization term that the authors describe as compatible with any existing GAN.

The method examines how sensitive the discriminator's prediction is to changes in its input. It compares the size of this gradient for real images with its size for generated samples, then encourages the gap between them to shrink. The target is therefore a difference in discriminator sensitivity across the two kinds of input.

The authors observe that this formulation helps avoid unfavorable attractors in the GAN optimization landscape and significantly improves training results with limited data. These are reported empirical findings, rather than a guarantee that every training run will avoid poor solutions. The approach matters because it supplies a broadly applicable modification focused on discriminator behavior when examples are scarce.
neurips-2022-diggan-discriminator-gradie.tldr: DigGAN improves limited-data GAN training by encouraging similar discriminator gradient magnitudes for real and generated images.

paragraphs: Fair ranking seeks useful rankings that also satisfy requirements about group representation. Those requirements can fail when the socially salient or protected attributes used to define groups contain errors. This paper studies how to build rankings while explicitly accounting for uncertainty in those attributes, instead of treating the recorded group information as exact.

The framework assumes attributes are perturbed randomly and independently. It combines probabilistic information about those perturbations with group fairness constraints. It can handle multiple overlapping attributes and a broad family of requirements, including proportional and equal representation. This scope allows the analysis to cover settings where an item belongs to more than one relevant group.

The authors prove guarantees for both fairness and utility, together with information-theoretic limits showing that these guarantees cannot be substantially improved under the model. Experiments find higher fairness than the compared baselines and a similar or better fairness–utility trade-off. The findings support incorporating attribute uncertainty directly into ranking, with the theoretical conclusions tied to the stated perturbation model.
neurips-2022-fair-ranking-with-noisy-pro.tldr: A ranking framework accounts for random, independent attribute errors and provides near-unimprovable fairness and utility guarantees under that model.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether an interface can learn to interpret a person's commands without action labels, reward feedback, an existing mapping, or knowledge of the intended task. Its guiding idea is that intuitive interfaces produce less noisy commands. The authors translate this idea into an objective measuring mutual information between commands and the changes they induce in the environment.

An observational study tests whether that score tracks interface effectiveness across typing, simulated robot control, and games using keyboard or eye-gaze inputs. Across 540,000 examples, the score predicts task-completion measures with an average Spearman rank correlation of 0.43. This supports its usefulness as an unsupervised signal without making it a perfect measure of success.

The authors then optimize randomly initialized interfaces through reinforcement learning while users attempt their tasks. Tests involve twelve participants controlling a cursor with a perturbed mouse and one expert playing Lunar Lander through webcam-recorded gestures. In these experiments, interfaces are learned from scratch with under thirty minutes of human-in-the-loop training.
neurips-2022-first-contact-unsupervised-.tldr: Maximizing mutual information between user commands and resulting state changes enables interface learning without task knowledge or explicit user supervision in the reported studies.

paragraphs: GET3D addresses the need to create many detailed and varied three-dimensional objects for virtual worlds. Its target output is an explicit textured mesh that a standard rendering engine can consume directly. That output format matters because a generated object needs usable geometry and surface appearance to fit into downstream 3D applications.

The model combines differentiable surface modeling, differentiable rendering, and ideas from two-dimensional generative adversarial networks. This combination enables training from collections of 2D images while producing 3D meshes. The generated shapes can have complex topology, detailed geometry, and high-quality textures, addressing several restrictions identified in previous approaches.

The paper reports high-quality generation across categories including cars, chairs, animals, motorbikes, human characters, and buildings, with significant improvements over earlier methods. The contribution therefore concerns both visual quality and the form in which the generated content is delivered. Learning from images produces assets designed for direct use in rendering software, connecting image-based training to practical 3D content creation.
neurips-2022-get3d-a-generative-model-of.tldr: GET3D learns from 2D image collections to generate detailed, textured 3D meshes that standard rendering engines can use directly.

paragraphs: Topic models seek interpretable themes within document collections. Embedded topic models represent words and topics in a geometric space, but the usual Euclidean space can make hierarchical relationships difficult to capture. HyperMiner changes that geometry to better represent how broad themes and more specific topics relate within a semantic hierarchy.

The framework embeds both words and topics in hyperbolic space, whose tree-like structure suits hierarchical data. This gives the model a way to exploit semantic relationships when discovering topics. The same geometry also provides a natural place to incorporate existing tree-structured knowledge rather than relying entirely on hierarchy discovery from documents.

To introduce that prior structure, the authors add a regularization term inspired by contrastive learning. It guides topic-hierarchy learning using the supplied structural knowledge. Experiments on topic taxonomy discovery and document representation show improvements over existing embedded topic models. The findings support choosing an embedding geometry that fits hierarchical organization and combining it with explicit structural guidance when available.
neurips-2022-hyperminer-topic-taxonomy-m.tldr: HyperMiner uses hyperbolic embeddings and optional structural guidance to improve topic hierarchy discovery and document representation.

paragraphs: People must balance exploring uncertain options with exploiting options they already know. This paper investigates the hypothesis that human exploration reflects good use of limited computational resources. It models the trade-off by allowing a learning algorithm to give up some task performance in exchange for a simpler implementation.

The authors meta-learn reinforcement learning algorithms while penalizing their description length, measured as the number of bits needed to implement them. This creates a family of models with different balances between performance and complexity. The resulting models capture human exploration behavior better than the previously considered Boltzmann, upper-confidence-bound, and Thompson-sampling approaches.

Changing the description-length allowance also produces behavior patterns related to differences in human cognition. Shorter descriptions capture behavior observed in brain-lesioned patients, while longer descriptions mirror cognitive development during adolescence. These results support the proposed resource-rational account as a model of behavior. They connect exploration patterns to computational constraints without establishing that the brain literally implements the learned algorithms.
neurips-2022-modeling-human-exploration-.tldr: Reinforcement learning models that trade performance for shorter descriptions better capture human exploration and related patterns of cognitive variation.

paragraphs: Auxiliary learning improves a primary task by training with additional losses that provide useful information. A single auxiliary loss, however, can help some parts of a network while harming others. This paper argues that balancing losses only at the whole-model level overlooks these different effects and can waste useful auxiliary information.

MAOAL assigns a learnable importance to each auxiliary loss for each model module. It jointly learns these importance values and the model parameters through two levels of optimization. The lower level updates model parameters using gradients shaped by the importance values. The upper level adjusts those values through implicit gradients from a small development dataset.

This arrangement makes the influence of auxiliary learning depend on where it acts within the network. Experiments across multiple datasets and auxiliary losses consistently outperform the state-of-the-art baselines considered in the paper. The results support module-specific control as a broadly useful way to improve auxiliary learning, rather than relying on one shared balance of losses for every network component.
neurips-2022-module-aware-optimization-f.tldr: MAOAL learns how strongly each auxiliary loss should influence each network module, improving auxiliary learning across the reported experiments.

paragraphs: A histogram distribution assigns constant probability within each of several intervals of an ordered domain. This paper studies whether samples alone can reveal if an unknown distribution has that structure. Specifically, the task is to distinguish a distribution representable with k intervals from one that is far from every such distribution in total variation distance.

The authors provide a computationally efficient testing algorithm whose sample requirements are nearly optimal. They also establish a lower bound showing that any tester needs nearly as many samples, with the upper and lower results differing only by logarithmic factors. This pairs an achievable procedure with evidence about the fundamental difficulty of the problem.

For a domain of size n and distance threshold epsilon, the sample complexity scales, up to logarithmic factors, as sqrt(nk)/epsilon + k/epsilon² + sqrt(n)/epsilon². The expression makes the roles of domain size, histogram complexity, and testing resolution explicit. The result characterizes the resources needed to test histogram structure, rather than requiring a full reconstruction of the unknown distribution.
neurips-2022-nearly-tight-bounds-for-tes.tldr: An efficient histogram-distribution tester and a nearly matching lower bound characterize the required sample count up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Continual learning systems often retain a small buffer of past examples and replay them during later training to reduce forgetting. This paper identifies a problem with that practice: repeatedly optimizing on a small memory can create tight, unstable decision boundaries. Remembering the stored examples can therefore come at the expense of generalization beyond that buffer.

The proposed method, Lipschitz-Driven Rehearsal, adds a surrogate objective that encourages smoother behavior in the network backbone. It constrains layer-wise Lipschitz constants with respect to replay examples, controlling how strongly layers can respond to changes around those examples. The approach targets the network's sensitivity during rehearsal.

Across multiple datasets, adding LiDER produces stable performance gains for several leading rehearsal methods, both with and without pretraining. Additional ablation experiments examine buffer overfitting and help characterize the regularizer's effect. These findings support smoothness control as a useful complement to retaining past data: the way a model learns from its memory matters alongside the presence of the memory itself.
neurips-2022-on-the-effectiveness-of-lip.tldr: LiDER constrains network sensitivity around replay examples to reduce buffer overfitting and improve rehearsal-based continual learning.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation aims to help a model trained on one data distribution perform well on another. Existing methods can be computationally expensive because training uses substantial source data. ORIENT tackles the efficiency problem by selecting a source subset that resembles the target data, concentrating training on examples relevant to the destination domain.

The framework uses submodular mutual information functions to make this selection. Its role is to choose training data for supervised domain adaptation methods, allowing those methods to work with a smaller source collection. The paper also shows how GLISTER, GRADMATCH, and CRAIG fit within the framework when they use a held-out query set.

Experiments combine ORIENT with d-SNE, CCSA, and standard cross-entropy training. These combinations produce both faster training and better target-domain performance in the reported evaluations. The results suggest that source-data selection can improve adaptation efficiency while also helping predictive quality. The connections to existing selection strategies make ORIENT a common framework for understanding several approaches to choosing relevant subsets.
neurips-2022-orient-submodular-mutual-in.tldr: ORIENT selects source examples similar to target data, yielding faster supervised domain adaptation and better target performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper gives theoretical conditions under which learning a shared representation across reinforcement learning tasks reduces data requirements. It works within low-rank Markov decision processes and assumes the upstream tasks share a common representation. The proposed reward-free multitask algorithm, REFUEL, learns transition models and near-optimal policies while producing a representation for later tasks.

The upstream benefit is conditional on having enough tasks: above a stated threshold, shared representation learning is provably more sample-efficient than learning each task independently. This identifies a regime where combining tasks provides a formal statistical advantage, rather than assuming that any amount of multitask training must help.

For a new task sharing the same representation, the authors develop sample-efficient methods in both online and offline settings. Their policy suboptimality bounds combine upstream representation-estimation error with a term that vanishes as downstream samples increase. More downstream data thus reduces one component of the bound while upstream representation quality remains relevant. These results also characterize the benefit over learning the low-rank representation directly downstream.
neurips-2022-provable-benefit-of-multita.tldr: Under a shared low-rank representation and sufficiently many tasks, REFUEL provides provable sample-efficiency benefits for upstream and downstream reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: A neural network can divide an image into regions, but producing a segmentation does not by itself quantify its statistical reliability. This paper treats the segmentation result as a hypothesis selected by the network. It then asks how to assess that hypothesis within a formal statistical testing framework.

The authors use conditional selective inference, which addresses hypotheses chosen using data. This is relevant because the network's output determines which segmentation hypothesis is evaluated. The method computes valid, exact p-values without relying on a large-sample approximation. The resulting significance assessment is attached to the network-driven hypothesis.

To make selective inference work for neural-network segmentation, the paper develops a homotopy-based algorithm that derives the hypothesis's exact sampling distribution. Several experiments demonstrate the proposed method's performance. The contribution adds a statistical assessment layer to segmentation: it evaluates the significance of a selected result rather than only producing the regions. Its central technical advance is making non-asymptotic inference available for these data-driven hypotheses.
neurips-2022-quantifying-statistical-sig.tldr: A homotopy-based selective inference method computes exact valid p-values for hypotheses derived from neural-network image segmentations.

paragraphs: Sampling from a distribution can become difficult when its variables obey constraints, its geometry is poorly conditioned, or its density is nonsmooth. This paper presents practical results for distributions combining these difficulties in dimensions exceeding 100,000. The goal is to make sampling workable in settings that are demanding both geometrically and computationally.

The algorithm incorporates constraints into Riemannian Hamiltonian Monte Carlo while preserving sparsity. Keeping the sparse structure is part of how the method handles very large problems. The authors report a mixing rate independent of smoothness and condition numbers, addressing two characteristics that otherwise make the target distributions challenging.

On systems-biology and linear-programming benchmarks, the method outperforms existing packages by orders of magnitude. For RECON3D, described as the largest published human metabolic network, it achieves a thousandfold speedup. The package has also been incorporated into a bioinformatics library. Together, the algorithmic result and benchmark evidence demonstrate practical sampling capability for the difficult high-dimensional distributions studied.
neurips-2022-sampling-with-riemannian-ha.tldr: A sparse, constrained Riemannian Hamiltonian Monte Carlo method enables efficient practical sampling in very high dimensions, including a thousandfold RECON3D speedup.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can accept graphs of different sizes, yet their classification accuracy can deteriorate when test graphs differ in size from training graphs. SizeShiftReg addresses this gap between architectural flexibility and learned generalization. It focuses on learning from smaller graphs and applying the resulting model to larger ones using only training data.

The method uses graph coarsening to simulate size changes within the training collection. A regularization objective then encourages the model to remain robust to those changes. This makes size variation part of the training signal without requiring access to graphs from the test domain or specifying a particular graph-generation process.

The authors describe the regularizer as applicable to any GNN. In experiments on standard datasets, popular models train on the smallest half of the graphs and are evaluated on the largest tenth. Adding SizeShiftReg yields performance improvements of up to thirty percent. These results support simulated training-time size shifts as a useful tool for improving generalization from small graphs to larger ones.
neurips-2022-sizeshiftreg-a-regularizati.tldr: SizeShiftReg simulates graph-size changes during training to improve GNN classification on larger graphs without accessing test data.

paragraphs: TGEA 2.0 is a dataset for diagnosing errors in text generated by pretrained language models. Its annotations go beyond marking a sentence as wrong: they locate problematic spans, classify errors through a two-level taxonomy, and identify words that explain the problem. This supports analysis of what failed and why.

The authors collect 170,000 prompts from six million natural sentences across three domains and use four generative models to produce paragraphs. Manual annotation covers 195,629 generated sentences, finding about 36,000 erroneous sentences and 42,000 erroneous spans. Each span receives a Minimal Set of Error-related Words, intended to capture both relevant words and the reasoning behind the error. Pre-annotation and feedback support quality control.

The dataset introduces five diagnostic tasks covering detection, explanatory-word extraction, span location, correction, and error classification, plus two mitigation tasks involving pairwise comparison and word prediction. Benchmark experiments show that these tasks remain challenging. The resource is designed to support research on identifying and reducing specific generation errors rather than assessing text quality only in aggregate.
neurips-2022-tgea-2-0-a-large-scale-diag.tldr: TGEA 2.0 provides detailed human annotations and seven benchmark tasks for diagnosing and mitigating errors in machine-generated text.

paragraphs: ROOTS is a large multilingual text corpus assembled through the BigScience collaboration. This paper documents the creation and curation work behind that resource, responding to the need for large, high-quality datasets as language models grow. The project frames data collection within a broader research effort that foregrounds ethics, potential harms, and governance.

The corpus contains 1.6 terabytes of text spanning 59 languages and was used to train BLOOM, a language model with 176 billion parameters. These figures establish both the scale of the data effort and its use in a concrete multilingual modeling project. The paper's focus is the dataset and the work required to assemble it.

The authors release a large initial subset of ROOTS together with analyses and provide processing tools intended to help other projects. They hope these resources support large-scale modeling in individual languages and across languages, as well as further study of the corpus itself. The contribution combines a substantial training-data resource with documentation and tools for subsequent research.
neurips-2022-the-bigscience-roots-corpus.tldr: ROOTS documents the curation of a 1.6-terabyte, 59-language corpus used to train BLOOM and releases an initial subset with supporting resources.

paragraphs: Visual Concepts Tokenization aims to turn an image into a set of representations that each capture an independent visual concept. The method is unsupervised and transformer-based, addressing both disentangled representation learning and scene decomposition. Its goal is to separate meaningful visual factors instead of allowing every representation to mix information about the entire image.

Concept tokens gather information from image tokens through cross-attention at successive layers. The architecture excludes self-attention between concept tokens to prevent information from passing directly among them. A separate Concept Disentangling Loss encourages different tokens to represent independent concepts. These components respectively help tokens acquire visual information and discourage overlap in what they represent.

Experiments across several datasets evaluate both disentangled representations and scene decomposition. The authors report state-of-the-art results by a large margin on the evaluated tasks. The findings support combining restrictions on information flow with a loss that encourages separation: the architecture controls how concepts are formed, while the objective pushes their representations toward distinct visual content.
neurips-2022-visual-concepts-tokenizatio.tldr: VCT combines isolated cross-attention pathways and a disentangling loss to learn separate visual concept tokens without supervision.

paragraphs: ZooD addresses how to choose and combine pretrained models for performance on unseen domains. Exhaustively fine-tuning model combinations is expensive, while selection must account for distribution shifts. The approach ranks models using their extracted features, then combines highly ranked candidates and selects useful features from the resulting ensemble.

Its ranking metric considers both separation between classes and stability across domains, assessed by leaving one training domain out at a time. After aggregating the top-ranked models, a variational expectation-maximization algorithm selects informative features. This second step aims to avoid accumulating noise simply because more models contribute to the ensemble.

Across a zoo of 35 models, the ranking better tracks fine-tuning rankings than previous methods and is up to 9,859 times faster than brute-force fine-tuning. The ensemble with feature selection outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods, raising DomainNet accuracy from 46.5% to 50.6%. The paper also supplies fine-tuning results for all 35 models on seven datasets, supporting further study of model selection under domain shift.
neurips-2022-zood-exploiting-model-zoo-f.tldr: ZooD efficiently ranks pretrained models and selects ensemble features to improve generalization to unseen domains.
